We leave additional ablation studies about the choice of target bias parameters and additional analysis of the VQ bottleneck in Appendix E . Component-wise Analysis. To demonstrate the effectiveness of each architectural component of HyperThink , we report the performance of its ablated variants in Table 3 . The first row corresponds to the System 2 Distillation baseline, which uses the same distillation objective and training data as HyperThink but fully fine-tunes the LLM. The second row restricts this baseline to optimizing only bias parameters, which can be viewed as global biases shared across queries. The large improvement over the first row highlights the robustness of bias parameters for steering a pretrained LLM. The third row is HyperThink without the VQ bottleneck, directly projecting the continuous outputs of the Bias Encoder to bias updates, and the last row is the full HyperThink . The results show that simply introducing query-specific test-time adaptation with the Text/Bias Encoders is insufficient to generalize the query-to-parameter mapping (Eq. ( 5 )). With the VQ decoder, HyperThink achieves much better out-of-distribution generalization on MATH-500, indicating that the discrete bottleneck acts as a strong regularizer against overfitting. To justify our choice, we compare variants of HyperThink using two common parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches: LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) and Prompt Tuning ( Lester et al., 2021 ) . We observe that both alternative parameterizations underperform bias adaptation, which supports the flexibility and robustness of bias-only tuning. Figure 7: Subject distribution and top keywords per VQ code. Analysis of the Learned VQ Codebook. To investigate the learned structure in the VQ codebook, we analyze whether similar problems are assigned the same VQ code. Figure 7 reports the distribution of subjects in MATH-500 for three representative VQ codes, along with the most frequent keywords in the problems assigned to each code. We observe that each code primarily covers related subjects. For example, the first code is mainly used for Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, Prealgebra, and Number Theory, and it is dominated by algebraic keywords such as “log” and “equation”. The second and third codes are used mainly for Probability and Precalculus, respectively, and are dominated by subject-related keywords. Overall, the alignment between subject-level assignments and code-specific lexical patterns suggests that individual VQ codes capture meaningful semantic structure in the math problem space. 5 Related Work Efficient Reasoning with Large Language Models.
